source.version_note: Despite the 2020 filename, this file is the40-page arXiv 1803.07170v2 preprint dated21 March2018, with a2018 title and full screenshot appendix. Cite the read version as2018. A related later Nature Human Behaviour article has DOI10.1038/s41562-019-0762-8, online28 October2019 and a2020 volume4(2) issue; its final text was not read here and is not counted as an independent replication.
source.verification_method: All 40 pages read: extracted main/reference/table text plus visual reading of every screenshot-only vignette/question pages 19–40. All 33 figures and all four tables inspected. arXiv verifies version/title/date; Crossref verifies metadata for the related later article. Narrow official-source checks inspect NHTSA closure/automation-level passages and the 2017 German commission’s rules 8–9, not the full reports or current law. No raw study data/code or final journal version was independently read.

citation.title: Blaming humans in autonomous vehicle accidents: Shared responsibility across levels of automation

reading.source_scope_note: Three U.S. MTurk vignette studies examine hypothetical car-control regimes, causal/blame ratings and limited competence appraisals. Methods report 786, 779 and 973 participants, with model subsets and exclusion/observation accounting needing clarification. This is an older preprint with a fully read image appendix, not a review of actual crash liability, juries, manufacturer prices or the later journal version.
access_limits: No raw data, code, condition-by-condition participant flow or final publication was independently read or reproduced. Cross-study MTurk uniqueness is not verified; exclusions require completion, near-perfect paragraph transcription and unique IDs within each study.

The appendix embeds its actual vignettes/questions as images; all were visually read rather than inferred from captions or falsely called extracted text. Evidence quotations below use searchable main-text passages.

NHTSA’s2017 closure cover and section4.1, and the German2017 commission’s rules8–9, were checked narrowly. Neither complete report, subsequent investigation, current law, cited book nor media narrative is claimed audited.

study.design: Study1: four between-person regimes HH,HM,MH,MM, with two within-person accident scenarios in random order. Study2: four regimes H,HM,MH,M crossed with car/company rating target, described as4×2 between-person. Study 3: same regimes crossed with car/company/programmer, described as4×3, but exact cell/sample accounting is not reproduced. Every person is described as seeing one Bad and one Missed Intervention scenario.
study.samples: Study1 reports786 U.S. MTurk participants, data September2017; Study2 reports779, data May2017; Study 3 reports973, date not stated in the read methods. Sum2,538 reported participations, not independently verified unique people or reconciled initial-versus-final flow. Table1 models use786/382/586 subjects; the latter two are labeled shared-control subsets.
study.clear_cases: Bad Intervention: first driver stays safely on course, secondary driver wrongly overrides into a pedestrian. Missed Intervention: first driver does not swerve away from a pedestrian, secondary driver also fails to override, despite an explicitly safe adjacent lane. Screens provide hazard knowledge, intervention capability and deterministic outcome. Case type changes number of errors, commission/omission, causal sequence and hazard setup together, not only one isolated error-count factor.
study.dilemmas: Study 3 changes the choice to one versus five deaths. In Bad Intervention, switching kills five instead of one; in Missed Intervention, not switching kills five instead of one. The latter raises the disputed permissibility of actively harming an initially unthreatened bystander; the authors explicitly acknowledge that fewer deaths is not an uncontested moral-correctness criterion.
study.measures: Separate0–100 judgments of blameworthiness and how much each target caused the death, independent rather than fixed-total shares. Single-item competence appears before accidents in Study1 and after each accident in Study2. Study1 HH/MM describe two distinct humans/programs; mixed regimes describe a primary actor and a secondary override. Later Industry aggregates different between-person car/company/programmer targets, rather than directly measuring a single institutional entity.
study.models: Table1 reports subject and question random effects. Bad models include human identity, mistake and their interaction; missed models include human identity, last-driver role and their interaction. Question type is pooled after a reported nonsignificant effect; two question categories are not two independent studies. Pairwise t tests and model observation counts need participant-cluster/aggregation clarification.
study.single_error_results: Mistake coefficients63.347(SE1.497),56.011(2.226),11.645(.939) for Studies1–3; human-identity coefficients1.192(1.500),1.810(2.226),−1.652(.939), with no displayed significance star. These are not equivalence tests. Error structure and contextual moral benchmark vary by study.
study.dual_error_results: Missed-intervention human coefficients17.321(SE1.628) and13.268(2.526) in Studies 1/2 favor human blame over machine/Industry. Role/main-effect and interaction estimates vary. In Study1, HM human77.65 versus machine53.45; MH human72.73 versus machine57.22. MM primary/secondary ratings67.51/68.53. Study2 full-machine Industry75.56 versus mixed MH59.50/HM48.52. These source means support a contextual rating pattern, not a normative proof that equal fault requires identical blame.
study.dilemma_results: Study 3 missed-intervention human coefficient2.341(SE.959), role−.244(.959), interaction2.782(1.356); the source calls driver type nonsignificant. Table1 stars only at.01,.001,.0001, so no star does not mean p>.05 or exact equality. No exact mixed-model p/df is supplied for that coefficient. Dilemma ratings are lower and source differences smaller than clear cases; do not claim identical effects or universal absence.
study.aggregation: The machine-machine comparison mean68.02 in prose pools the role means67.51/68.53, rather than being exactly the primary-role mean. Many pairwise dfs are large relative to expected unique-person condition counts and may reflect pooled repeated ratings; original contrasts are needed before treating every comparison as a valid independent-person t test.
study.reporting_conflicts: The Bad-Intervention means human53.36/machine49.78 closely reconcile with pooled Study1 roles: using approximate HM/MH weights .496/.504 gives .496×19.30+.504×86.90≈53.36 and .496×83.85+.504×16.21≈49.78. This is a transparent reconstruction from rounded Table2 means, not a raw-data reproduction. It mixes correct and erring targets and should not be called an error-only contrast. Separately, Table1 Study 3 prints586 subjects and4,688 observations per case, eight each, although methods/appendix specify four questions per case. Case filtering/counts still need original output.
study.competence: Figure3 compares before ratings from Study1 with after ratings from a different Study2 sample, collected in a different month and with different representative conditions. Similar source means do not establish exact equivalence, no mediation, within-person change or a causal effect of timing.
study.policy_scope: Arguments about jury regulation, product liability, prices, adoption, incentives and accident-related media reactions are extrapolations. No jury deliberation, legal standard, real operator performance, strategic blame avoidance, corporate response or comparative regulatory intervention is tested.

summary: No new term. Enrich blame and retrospective causal attribution from the exact 2018 preprint, preserving single-error/dilemma boundaries and car/Industry pooling. Keep crumple-zone, responsibility-gap, scapegoating and competence explanations qualified. Correct contemporaneous Autopilot level, NHTSA date/closure scope and an omitted commission qualifier; flag sample/observation, contrast and threshold ambiguities without inventing raw fixes.

findings.definition: Assigning fault or responsibility to an agent for a negative event or outcome.
findings.novelty_rationale: An existing attribution concept or boundary covers this evidence. Do not create a new mechanism label for a context-dependent rating contrast.

evidence.quote: the machine driver is consistently blamed less than the human
When only one agent makes an error
the reason that subjects blame machine drivers less than human

findings.evidence_scope: Three vignette studies compare shared-control and single-driver vehicles. In the clear dual-error cases of Studies 1/2, pooled blame/causal-responsibility ratings are lower for the machine/Industry target than the human; single-error and dilemma patterns differ. Industry pools car/company and, in Study 3, programmer ratings. The exact 2018 preprint, rather than the 2020 final journal text, was read. Reporting, threshold and clustering questions limit exact inference.
findings.boundary: Attributed blame, causal contribution, corporate accountability and legal liability differ. No error-free human is necessarily being scapegoated: shared-control vignettes explicitly give both actors information and intervention ability. Lower machine ratings do not prove a conserved blame transfer or uniquely identify the psychological cause.

findings.definition: A retrospective assessment of an agent’s causal contribution to an outcome that occurred.
findings.novelty_rationale: An existing attribution concept or boundary covers this evidence. Do not create a new mechanism label for a context-dependent rating contrast.

evidence.quote: to what degree each of these two agents caused

findings.evidence_scope: Participants separately rate how much each target caused the death on 0–100 scales, then the authors pool causal and blame ratings after reporting no question effect. This is retrospective causal attribution, but the combined source-type estimates cannot be treated as independent, pure causal-pivotality effects or a validated necessity/sufficiency metric.
findings.boundary: Perceived causal contribution does not settle moral fault, legal duty or justified punishment. No mean question effect is not proof that causal responsibility and blame are interchangeable; independent non-zero-sum ratings are not shares of a fixed responsibility budget.

findings.definition: A pattern in which a human operator bears disproportionate blame or responsibility for failure in a complex automated system despite having limited control over its actions.
findings.novelty_rationale: An existing attribution concept or boundary covers this evidence. Do not create a new mechanism label for a context-dependent rating contrast.

evidence.quote: some amount of blame was attributed to machines and humans who were not even in the decision-making loop

findings.evidence_scope: Boundary only: shared-control observers often rate the human above Industry in clear dual-error cases, and fully autonomous passengers receive some blame despite no described intervention role. Those patterns raise an attribution question but do not establish disproportionate real operator liability relative to information/control. In the shared-control vignettes, the human is explicitly able to see the hazard and intervene.
findings.boundary: Higher human blame is not by itself an unfair crumple zone. Establish actual authority, time, knowledge, duty and normative proportionality; hypothetical ratings and a speculative policy mechanism do not establish real scapegoating.

findings.definition: A shortfall in the responsibility attributed to actors considered capable of bearing it when an artificial agent is involved in a shared outcome.
findings.novelty_rationale: An existing attribution concept or boundary covers this evidence. Do not create a new mechanism label for a context-dependent rating contrast.

evidence.quote: drop in machine responsibility in cases where a human and machine share control of the car is also verified in Study 2

findings.evidence_scope: Boundary only: the main contrast concerns diminished machine/Industry ratings in human–machine dual-error cases, not a measured sum of responsibility across every eligible human/institution. Industry itself pools distinct targets. Do not equate this with a demonstrated human-only responsibility shortfall or actual accountability gap.
findings.boundary: A decrease for one target is not conserved transfer, nobody accountable or justified human exoneration. The existing gap definition and its aggregation assumptions require separate tests.

findings.definition: Deflecting personal or collective responsibility for a negative outcome by directing blame toward another person, group or entity.
findings.novelty_rationale: An existing attribution concept or boundary covers this evidence. Do not create a new mechanism label for a context-dependent rating contrast.

evidence.quote: people may train themselves to drive in a way that, if they
crash, the blame is likely to fall to the machine

findings.evidence_scope: Boundary only: strategic driving or reliance to shift later blame is a discussion conjecture. Respondents judge fictional third parties; no driver chooses a system, changes conduct to evade sanctions, or deliberately deflects responsibility in the experiments.
findings.boundary: Prospective incentives, observed blame ratings and an actor’s deliberate evasion differ. Legitimately assigning a machine or company a causal role is not automatically scapegoating.

findings.definition: Expecting an agent or system to perform competently and reliably in a relevant task.
findings.novelty_rationale: An existing attribution concept or boundary covers this evidence. Do not create a new mechanism label for a context-dependent rating contrast.

evidence.quote: assessments of competence did not mediate
ratings were collected before participants read about

findings.evidence_scope: Boundary only: Studies 1/2 ask single-item perceived driving competence, before accidents in one sample and after in another. Similar ratings do not establish equivalent task performance, no competence pathway or calibrated reliance. These are not actual trust/reliance decisions, and the before/after display compares different studies and collection dates.
findings.boundary: Capability appraisal, reliance, moral standing and warranted accountability differ. Null perceived-competence contrasts do not prove zero mediation; no independently randomized competence mediator or complete causal mediation analysis is supplied.

source_corrections.issue: The filename labels the source2020, but its header and version record identify arXiv 1803.07170v2,21 March2018.
source_corrections.resolution: Cite the read title/version as2018. Link the later article only as related publication metadata and do not transfer all preprint criticisms or claim that its final text was reviewed. Avoid treating versions as independent empirical replications.

source_corrections.issue: The preprint maps Tesla Autopilot toL3.
source_corrections.resolution: The contemporaneous NHTSA report section4.1 identifies L1 with cruise control and L2 with Autosteer. Treat the experiment’s control regimes as abstractions; do not identify that real product asL3.

source_corrections.issue: The report is cited2016 and paraphrased as finding Tesla not at fault.
source_corrections.resolution: The cited closing report is dated19 January2017. It closes a defect evaluation and expressly preserves the possibility of a safety defect; this is not complete exoneration. Correct the agency name to National Highway Traffic Safety Administration. Only the relevant cover/section passages were checked.

source_corrections.issue: An ellipsis omits rule9’s conditional allowance for general programming to reduce personal injury, while the prose suggests a blanket prohibition on life tradeoffs.
source_corrections.resolution: Restore the qualified context: rule9 says general injury-reduction programming may be justifiable, while prohibiting personal-feature distinctions and sacrificing uninvolved people. Rule8 also stresses contextual dilemmas. Neither unrestricted utilitarian permission nor an unqualified ban on all harm minimization follows. This is a narrow check of2017 guidance, not a current statutory-law audit.

source_corrections.location: Page7 Table1 and pages13/36–37, Study 3 observations
source_corrections.issue: Table1 lists586 subjects and4,688 observations for each case-specific model. The methods and visible questionnaire specify four ratings per case, or2,344 for586 subjects;4,688 corresponds to both cases combined.
source_corrections.resolution: Request the actual model datasets, question counts, case filters and sample flow. The report is unreconciled; it does not prove duplicated data or justify a guessed corrected N.

source_corrections.location: Page8, pooled Bad-Intervention contrast versus Appendix Table2
source_corrections.issue: The text uses human53.36/machine49.78 near a claim about erring agents. Those values are consistent with pooling correct and erring roles from Study1, rather than an error-only comparison.
source_corrections.resolution: Approximate HM/MH weights .496/.504 reconstruct the reported means from Table2: human19.30/86.90 and machine83.85/16.21. Do not flag the means as impossible or compare them only with Study2. Clarify the pooled estimand and obtain a participant-clustered error-status-specific contrast. This arithmetic check does not reproduce the raw analysis.

source_corrections.issue: No stars and nonsignificant source/competence comparisons are described as no effect or equal competence. The table displays thresholds only at1% or stricter, and the dilemma human coefficient is2.341 withSE.959.
source_corrections.resolution: State the displayed estimates and declared thresholds. A missing star is not evidence for p>.05, equivalence, zero effect or no causal mediation. Exact model tests/df and a mediation specification are required.

source_corrections.issue: Different-study competence comparisons are described as equal before/after drops, and hypothetical public ratings are used to predict jury outcomes and regulatory effectiveness.
source_corrections.resolution: Separate cross-study descriptives from within-person or randomized timing effects. Keep regulation, adoption/pricing and incentive consequences as proposals requiring independent evidence, not validated outcomes of these experiments.

source_identity_checks.scope: Crossref metadata identifies the same eight-author group, Drivers are blamed more than their automated cars when both make mistakes, Nature Human Behaviour 4(2), 134–143. Article online date is 28 October 2019; the nested journal-issue record is February 2020. The final text and version-level changes were not read, and no additional independent study credit is assigned.

methodological_limits: U.S. MTurk respondents rate stylized fictional accidents with stipulated outcomes and perfect knowledge/intervention options. They are not operating a car, investigating a real crash or deciding an actual legal case.
Case type bundles error count, action/inaction, causal sequence and hazard context. The contrast does not isolate one unique responsibility-dilution or omission mechanism.

The existence of two errors does not establish equal moral standing, duty or deserved blame. Human and machine/company targets differ substantively, and no independent normative fairness benchmark is supplied.

Blame and causal contribution are measured separately but pooled after a reported null question effect. Similar average results do not make their concepts identical; independent rating scales need not sum to100.

Industry combines machine, company and sometimes programmer ratings across different respondents. A pooled effect cannot automatically be attributed uniquely to the machine or its manufacturer, and an institutional representative is not equivalent to a mental machine agent.

Reported participant totals, model subsets and response counts need fuller reconciliation. One pair of means can be explained by pooling correct and erring roles; that pooled contrast still needs appropriate participant clustering and must not be presented as an error-only test. No unverified sample repair is made.

Stars use stricter thresholds than the common.05 criterion. No star, no detected contrast and exact equality are different claims; the dilemma result should retain its nonzero estimate and unclear exact test.

Competence timing varies across separate studies and participant samples, not an isolated randomized or within-person pre/post factor. A null competence-source contrast does not establish absence of mediation or actual equal capability.

The dilemma benchmark prioritizes fewer deaths in coding, but the authors acknowledge competing duties to uninvolved people. Neither public preference nor a reported null source effect determines the ethically correct driving policy.

The human in shared-control cases is explicitly informed and able to intervene; real workload, confusion, limited time, hidden failures and organizational power are not modeled. Some blame for a fully autonomous passenger raises a further question but does not adjudicate proportionality.

Observed attribution differs from deliberate scapegoating, felt diffusion, an institutional responsibility vacuum or an effective remedy. Proposed strategic nonintervention and social incentives are not enacted behavior.

Crash anecdotes and correspondence to them do not establish external validity of juries, media response, manufacturer pricing or federal-preemption proposals. Historical/legal claims and cited books were not fully audited.

The reviewed source is the2018 preprint. Publication metadata for a later version and narrow official-report excerpts do not constitute a full read of those works or a current legal/technical certification.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Awad’s contextual dual-error contrast differs from a simple autonomous-robot label effect. Both involve perceived blame, and the former’s dilemma conditions do not establish universal human/machine parity or a unique agency explanation.

Non-zero-sum ratings of self, machine and corporate actors are not conserved responsibility transfers. Competence perceptions, actual reliance, control and deserved accountability must remain separate.
Sample/model dfs, composite constructs and profession/source labels need explicit scope. A convincing narrative cannot repair unreconciled observation counts or turn belief into demonstrated agency.
Preserve source-version identity and do not replace a read preprint or valid conference version with a different final article merely because filenames or years suggest another citation.

That earlier review already identified the 2018 preprint and later journal article as related source leads without claiming a full read. This review supplies the complete preprint reading, including image-only materials; it does not convert the later article into a second replication.

deferred.reason: A useful contextual result, already covered by blame/causal attribution. The source explicitly leaves the mechanism open; do not add a redundant mechanism label.

deferred.term: Moral crumple zone / scapegoating / diffusion / responsibility gap
deferred.reason: Higher human ratings, pooled Industry decreases and speculative future incentives do not establish those distinct psychological or institutional conditions. Existing entries receive boundary notes where relevant.

The paper measures blame, causal responsibility and limited perceived competence, not a distinct mental-state mediator or actual machine agency. Future-work suggestions do not become established mechanisms.

deferred.term: Federal-preemption superiority / juror bias / autonomous-car adoption
deferred.reason: Policy and market extrapolations, not outcomes tested in the vignette experiments.

limitations: All 40 supplied pages were read, including every image-only vignette/question page, all 33 figures, four tables and references. No raw dataset, full official report, final journal version or cited book is claimed read; no author was contacted.
No new row, forced citation quota, annual count or automatic ethical/harm edge is added. Source corrections explicitly concern the read preprint, and unresolved analyses remain unresolved.
